title: Partition of India (1947) — players, timeline, POV, and sources

scope.included: Political, administrative, and communal-leadership actors who influenced the 1947 partition decision, boundary drawing, or immediate violence/migration—not post-hoc artists, filmmakers, or historians. Includes princelyStateActors roster with one-line roles and accession outcomes.
scope.excluded: Literary and artistic depictions; modern commemoration unless politically relevant.
scope.geographicFocus: British India partition into Dominion of India and Dominion of Pakistan (includes Punjab, Bengal, NWFP referendum, princely states accession crises).
scope.casualtyNote: Death estimates in partition violence remain disputed (~200,000 to 2 million in scholarly literature cited on Wikipedia).

nationalityGuide.britishIndianSubject: Legal nationality of most South Asians under the Raj until dominion independence in August 1947.
nationalityGuide.after1947: Dominion citizenship of India (from 15 Aug 1947) or Pakistan (from 14 Aug 1947); princely rulers chose accession.
nationalityGuide.labelingConvention: Fields use primary (colonial), afterAugust1947 (where applicable), and ethnicOrRegionalIdentity for community context—not equivalent to modern passport nationality.

twoNationTheory.summary: Claim that Hindus and Muslims are separate nations; foundation of Pakistan Movement; also echoed by Hindu Mahasabha figures.

populationExchange.summary: Full exchange (all Muslims to Pakistan, all Hindus/Sikhs to India) advocated by Patel and Ambedkar; rejected by Gandhi and Nehru. Punjab saw de facto massive exchange amid violence.

britishMotivations.summary: Post-war exhaustion, Labour anti-imperialism, fear of civil war, and desire for quick exit; debates on whether haste increased violence.

princelyStatesGuide.definition: Semi-autonomous kingdoms under British paramountcy—not British provinces. Rulers (maharajas, nawabs, nizams) governed internally; Britain handled external relations until paramountcy lapsed on 15 Aug 1947.
princelyStatesGuide.legalChange1947: Indian Independence Act ended paramountcy; rulers were expected to accede to India or Pakistan via Instrument of Accession (defence, foreign affairs, communications to chosen dominion).
whyTheyMatterForPartition: They were not divided by the Radcliffe Line but chose (or were pressured to choose) India or Pakistan.
Several rulers or their governments participated in communal violence or failed to stop it (especially Rajputana and Punjab border states).
Delayed or contested accessions (Kashmir, Hyderabad, Junagadh) extended 1947 crisis into wars and police actions in 1947–48.
princelyStatesGuide.integratorsNote: All-India accession campaign on the Indian side was driven mainly by Sardar Patel and civil servant V. P. Menon (not princely rulers).

rolesDelineationAndLegacyToPresent.summary: 1947 produced today’s South Asian map through two separate mechanisms: (A) negotiators who split British provinces and created India/Pakistan dominions, and (B) princely rulers and local actors who chose which dominion to join—or resisted—plus communal violence that changed who lived where. Today’s borders, disputes, and demographic realities are the stacked result of both layers—not princely accession alone, and not the Radcliffe Line alone.

mechanismA_provincialPartition.label: Main authors — provincial partition & dominion creation
whatItDetermined: Existence of two successor states: Dominion of India and Dominion of Pakistan (later Republic of India, Islamic Republic of Pakistan, and after 1971 People's Republic of Bangladesh).
Split of Punjab and Bengal provinces along roughly communal-majority district lines (Radcliffe Line).
Referenda: NWFP to Pakistan; Sylhet (Assam) to East Pakistan.
Division of British Indian Army, treasury, railways, and civil service.
Legal end of British Raj on 14–15 August 1947.
whatItDidNotDetermine: Borders of most princely states (they acceded as units, then merged).
Final status of Kashmir, Hyderabad, Junagadh without later accession wars/plebiscites.
Exact population mix on each side—violence and migration reshaped demographics after the legal line was drawn.

primaryActorGroups.role: Escalated Punjab communal war; ideological two-nation mirror—shaped facts on ground before Radcliffe published.

mechanismB_princelyAccessionAndLocalViol.label: Princely states & local sovereigns — accession, integration, cleansing
whatItDetermined: Which dominion inherited each princely territory (India vs Pakistan)—adding pieces not covered by provincial Radcliffe cuts.
Post-1947 map of Indian Union after Patel–Menon integration (~562 states into India; Pakistani states into Pakistan).
Local demographic shocks (Meo expulsions from Rajputana/Sikh states; Sindh Hindu exodus) on top of Punjab/Bengal migration.
Unresolved or disputed territories: Kashmir (Hari Singh accession + war), Hyderabad (1948), Junagadh (plebiscite), Kalat (Balochistan).
whatItDidNotDetermine: Creation of Pakistan as a concept—that came from League + provincial partition.
East vs West Pakistan wings—the eastern wing was Bengal province partition, not a princely state decision.

primaryActorGroups.role: Pressed accession to India or Pakistan; standstill agreements; prevented independent Hyderabad long-term.
Rulers’ hesitation or independence bids became today’s Kashmir dispute and settled but traumatic integrations.
Acceded to India while participating in or enabling Muslim expulsion—reinforced near-total Muslim exit from East Punjab.
Mass Meo Muslim flight into Pakistan from regions not drawn on Radcliffe map—shows violence ≠ only provincial border.
Expanded Pakistan beyond Punjab/Sindh province lines; Kalat foreshadows Baloch grievances.
Small Muslim-majority pocket surviving in Indian Punjab—proves map + accession ≠ uniform cleansing.
